scenes.title: Where does this line cross the x-axis?
body: Key question: what is y on the x-axis?
scenes.narration: Suppose the line is two x plus three y equals twelve, and you need its x-intercept. Here’s the idea: an intercept is not a formula trick. It is a location on an axis. So before doing algebra, ask what must be true at every point on the x-axis.

scenes.title: The x-axis forces y = 0
body: Every point on the x-axis has y = 0
Common mistake: setting x = 0 finds the y-intercept
scenes.narration: Every point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of zero. That is why we set y equal to zero when finding an x-intercept. This is where students often mix things up: setting x equal to zero finds the y-intercept. For the x-intercept, it is y that must be zero.

scenes.title: Use the axis condition in the equation
scenes.narration: Now substitute y equals zero into the original equation. We get two x plus three times zero equals twelve, so two x equals twelve. Notice why this works: we are restricting the equation to points that lie on the x-axis, then asking which x-value still satisfies the line.

scenes.title: Solve and interpret the result
scenes.narration: Divide both sides by two, and x equals six. But if the question asks for the x-intercept, do not stop at the number six. The intercept is the point six comma zero, because that is the actual point where the line meets the x-axis.

scenes.title: Quick check: does the point belong to the line?
body: Idea: x-intercept means y = 0, then solve for x
scenes.narration: Quick check: substitute six comma zero into the original equation. Two times six plus three times zero equals twelve, so the point works. Recap the idea: the x-intercept is where the graph meets the x-axis, every point there has y equal to zero, so set y equal to zero and solve for x. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT.
